name: Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value
principle: Code uses an untrusted or miscomputed size directly in a memory allocation without enforcing an upper bound. A large or unsigned-wrapped value can exhaust heap or stack memory and cause denial of service.
detection_signals: malloc(size), calloc(count, size), realloc(ptr, size), new char[size], or alloca(size) where size comes from input
C99 variable length array declaration like char buf[len] where len is input-derived or arithmetic-derived
std::vector<T> v(n), vector.resize(n), string.reserve(n), or new T[n] using unbounded n
Java new byte[size], new int[size], Arrays.copyOf(arr, size), ByteBuffer.allocate(size), or new HashMap(size) using untrusted size
size_t len = signed_expr or subtraction result followed by allocation with len
allocation size computed as count * sizeof(T) or a - b with no maximum-size check before allocation
array or collection index assignment that auto-expands storage using an untrusted large index
negative_signals: explicit check size <= MAX_ALLOC_SIZE before every allocation influenced by size
explicit check count <= MAX_COUNT && elem_size <= MAX_ELEM_SIZE before count * elem_size allocation
checked multiplication helper such as __builtin_mul_overflow or safe_mul before allocation and max bound check after
input size is clamped with min(requested, MAX_ALLOWED) before allocation
streaming or chunked processing uses fixed-size buffers instead of allocating requested total size
Java constructor rejects size > configuredMax before new byte[size] or new HashMap(size)
false_defense_traps: checking only size >= 0 while allowing huge positive values
checking only malloc result for NULL after requesting attacker-controlled memory
using unsigned size_t does not prevent negative-to-huge conversion
catching OutOfMemoryError without preventing the excessive allocation request
system memory limits reduce system impact but can still crash or terminate the process
verification_focus: Can an attacker control or influence an allocation size that is not bounded to a safe application-defined maximum before allocation?

consequence_chains.trigger: specified quantity from input is accepted without an upper bound
consequence_chains.consequence: excessive heap or stack allocation causes memory exhaustion

consequence_chains.trigger: large unvalidated array index forces automatic array or collection growth
consequence_chains.consequence: process exits or crashes from out-of-memory

consequence_chains.trigger: excessive allocation fails and returned NULL is dereferenced
consequence_chains.consequence: application crash and denial of service

patch_principle: Validate every allocation-influencing input against a documented maximum before allocation.
Reject or clamp requests that exceed configured memory limits.
Use checked arithmetic for allocation size calculations before multiplying or subtracting.
Prefer fixed-size, pooled, streaming, or chunked processing for attacker-sized data.
Configure OS/container memory limits as a secondary containment control.

minimal_examples.safe: size_t n = GetUntrustedInt(); if (n > MAX_ALLOC) return ERROR; char *buf = malloc(n);
